Effect Sizes and Model Checks from Permutations

Source: R/perm-stats.R
permstats.Rd

Uses the permuted statistics kept by permmodels to give, for each term and coefficient, a standardised effect size and a check of the usual parametric test against the permutation distribution.

Usage

permstats(x, level = 0.05)

Arguments

x

A result of permmodels with Freedman-Lane permutations (method = "auto", the default, or "freedman-lane").

level

The significance level of the check of the parametric test (default 0.05).

Value

A data frame with one row per term and coefficient (rows "coef:<name>"):

statistic

the observed statistic: F for terms, |t| for coefficients (robust ones with robust = TRUE).

df1, df2

numerator and denominator df of the usual parametric test: the residual df for lm, aov, glm and gls, Satterthwaite df for lmer, nlme's df for lme, and Inf (Wald chi-square) for glmer and glmmTMB.

p.param

the parametric p-value of the observed statistic with these df.

p.perm

the permutation p-value (as in the tables of permmodels()).

ses

the standardised effect size, (observed - mean of the permuted statistics) / their standard deviation (Gotelli and McCabe 2002): how far the observed statistic lies from what the permutations give when the effect is absent, in standard deviations.

param.size

the proportion of permuted data sets in which the parametric test rejects at level. The permuted data sets have no effect for the tested term, so this is the type I error rate of the parametric test for data like these: close to level when the parametric reference distribution suits the data, clearly above it when the parametric test is too liberal here (for example with unequal variances, overdispersion or few groups), below it when it is conservative. With few permutations it is rough (its standard error is about sqrt(level (1 - level) / nperm)).

Details

Every permuted data set comes from the model without the tested term (Freedman-Lane), so the permuted statistics show how the statistic behaves when that term has no effect but everything else in the data is kept. Comparing the parametric p-value with the permutation p-value, and param.size with level, shows whether the usual test can be trusted for these data. For mixed models the permuted statistics are Wald statistics (unadjusted covariance), so param.size checks the Wald F with the given df, not the Kenward-Roger test.

References

Gotelli, N. J. and McCabe, D. J. (2002). Species co-occurrence: a meta-analysis of J. M. Diamond's assembly rules model. Ecology, 83, 2091-2096.

Author

Dongwen Luo, Siva Ganesh and John Koolaard

Examples

mtcars$cyl <- factor(mtcars$cyl)
fm <- lm(mpg ~ wt + cyl, data = mtcars)
pfl <- permmodels(fm, nperm = 999, type = "II", seed = 1, prt = FALSE)
permstats(pfl)
#>           statistic df1 df2      p.param p.perm       ses param.size
#> wt        18.080056   1  28 0.0002130435  0.001 11.695665 0.04904905
#> cyl        7.285567   2  28 0.0028353022  0.005  4.622323 0.05705706
#> coef:wt    4.252065   1  28 0.0002130435  0.001  5.599425 0.04904905
#> coef:cyl6  3.070244   1  28 0.0047178339  0.009  3.291703 0.05905906
#> coef:cyl8  3.674214   1  28 0.0009991893  0.003  4.186066 0.05405405
